questions.statement: Choose the correct option to express a future plan already decided: "Next January, we _______ to Bariloche. We already bought the tickets."
questions.context: Martina y su familia están planeando sus próximas vacaciones de verano.

options.feedback: "Will" is used for spontaneous decisions and promises made at the moment of speaking, not for a plan whose tickets are already bought.
A fixed plan with the date and place already arranged takes the present continuous, "are going", and the bought tickets are the proof of that arrangement.
The bare present simple is used for timetables such as train departures, not for a personal holiday plan.
The present continuous needs both parts: the auxiliary "are" plus the -ing form, so "going" alone leaves the verb unfinished.

questions.explanation:
Cuando ya tenés los pasajes en la mano (como Martina para ir al sur), lo más natural es usar el presente continuo con sentido de futuro: "We are going". Indica que el plan está súper firme y organizado.

questions.statement: For a spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking, which form is correct? "Oh, we don't have any yerba mate. I _______ to the kiosk to buy some."
questions.context: Facundo está en la cocina y se da cuenta de que no hay más yerba.

options.feedback: "Will" is the form used for a decision taken at the very moment of speaking, which is exactly what happens when the yerba mate is found to be missing.
"Be going to" expresses an intention you already had before speaking, but here the plan is made on the spot.
The present continuous marks an organized arrangement, and this decision was sudden, so it does not fit.
The bare present simple is not used for spontaneous decisions about the future.

questions.explanation:
Si te das cuenta de algo y decidís actuar en el momento (como ir a comprar yerba), usás "will". Es la forma típica para las reacciones rápidas ante una situación presente.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When making a prediction based on what we see (evidence), which structure is preferred? "Look at those dark clouds! It _______ rain."
questions.context: Un pronóstico meteorológico para la zona de CABA y alrededores.

options.feedback: "Will" carries predictions based on opinion or general knowledge; here the evidence is right in front of the speaker, so "is going to" is preferred.
"Be going to" is the structure for a prediction based on visible evidence, and the dark clouds are exactly that evidence.
"Is raining" states that it is already raining, but the clouds only show that it is about to happen.
The bare present simple is not used for an immediate weather prediction.

questions.explanation:
Si ves las nubes negras sobre el Obelisco, tenés evidencia de que va a llover. En ese caso, la regla dice que debés usar "is going to rain". Guardá el "will" para cuando creas que va a llover pero no tengas la prueba frente a tus ojos.

questions.statement: Choose the best option for an intention (something you want to do but haven't organized yet): "Next year, I _______ study Architecture at the University of Córdoba."
questions.context: Lucía habla sobre sus metas académicas para el próximo año en Córdoba.

options.feedback: "Will" sounds like a promise made on the spot rather than a goal that has been planned for years.
"Be going to" is the form used for intentions and personal projects that have not been fully organized yet.
The bare present simple would describe a current routine, and the sentence has no marker of future time in the verb.
"Am studying" would suggest an arrangement already settled, with the enrolment closed and a full schedule.

questions.explanation:
Para tus sueños o proyectos (como la carrera que querés seguir), usás "am going to". Indica que ya lo estuviste pensando y que es tu intención firme hacerlo.

questions.statement:
What does the waiter say when a customer decides what to eat?
Customer: "I'll have the empanadas, please."
Waiter: "Excellent choice. I _______ them to you in a minute."
questions.context: Un mozo en un restaurante de Mendoza toma un pedido.

options.feedback: "Am bringing" points to an arrangement already planned, but this is a reply to a customer's order.
"Will" is the form used for an offer to do something or an immediate promise, which is what the waiter is making here.
The bare present simple does not sound natural for a promise of a future action in this service context.
It would be understood, but "will" is far more common for this kind of service offer than "am going to".

questions.explanation:
En un restaurante, los ofrecimientos de los mozos y los pedidos de los clientes casi siempre van con "will" ('ll). Es una forma de decir "lo voy a hacer ahora mismo por vos".

questions.statement: Fill in the blanks with the correct future forms: "We _______ (have) an asado on Sunday. I _______ (buy) the meat on Friday, I already talked to the butcher."
questions.context: Un grupo de amigos organiza una juntada para comer un asado el domingo.

options.feedback: "Will" sounds too uncertain for a barbecue that is already being organised, with the butcher already spoken to.

options.text: are having / am going to buy
options.feedback: The social event with a fixed day uses the present continuous "are having", and buying the meat is a firm intention, "am going to buy".
"Have" and "buy" with no auxiliary describe routines, not one specific event planned for this Sunday.

options.text: are going to have / will buy
options.feedback: It could work, but the second half is more a firm intention than a decision taken spontaneously, so it is not the best pair.

questions.explanation:
Para organizar una salida o reunión (como un asado), lo más común es el presente continuo ("are having"). Y para las tareas que ya sabés que tenés que hacer para ese evento, usás "am going to".

questions.statement: For predictions about the distant future based on opinion, which is more appropriate? "I think that in 2050, most cars in Argentina _______ electric."
questions.context: Una discusión sobre el futuro de la tecnología en Argentina hacia el año 2050.

options.feedback: "Will" is the form used after verbs of opinion such as "I think" for long-range predictions.
"Going to" is preferred for the near future or when there is evidence, not for abstract opinions about 2050.
"Are being" is a present continuous form and makes no sense in a prediction set in the year 2050.
The bare infinitive "be" has no future auxiliary, so the sentence would be grammatically incomplete.

questions.explanation:
Cuando das tu opinión sobre cómo va a ser el mundo dentro de mucho tiempo ("I think..."), lo mejor es usar "will". Es el futuro de las ideas y las creencias personales.

questions.statement: Select the sentence that correctly uses the Present Simple for a future timetable:
questions.context: El uso del presente simple para el futuro en horarios de transporte en Buenos Aires.

options.text: I am leaving for Mendoza tomorrow morning.
options.feedback: "I am leaving" is a personal plan, so it correctly uses the present continuous rather than a timetable.

options.text: The train to Tigre leaves in ten minutes from Retiro station.
options.feedback: Public transport timetables use the present simple for departures, which is exactly what this sentence does.
It does use the present simple, but "I think" marks an opinion rather than the official schedule.
"Will leave" is a general prediction, not the specific use of a fixed timetable.

questions.explanation:
Acordate siempre: para trenes, aviones, colectivos o funciones de teatro, usás el presente simple aunque hables del futuro. Es "The train leaves", no importa si falta una hora. Es una regla de oro para viajar por Argentina.

questions.statement:
Compare these two sentences:
1. "I will help you with your homework later."
2. "I am going to help you with your homework later."
Which one sounds like a formal promise or an offer made right now?
questions.context: Distinguir entre una promesa y una intención en un diálogo.

options.feedback: "Will" is the tense used for promises and for offers made spontaneously at the moment of speaking, which is what sentence 1 does.
Sentence 2 sounds like a plan you had already decided on before being asked.
They are not identical: "will" commits at the moment of speaking while "am going to" points to a prior intention.
Both sentences are grammatically correct; only the communicative nuance differs.

questions.explanation:
Si querés quedar bien y prometerle algo a alguien en el momento ("Te prometo que te ayudo"), usás "will". El "going to" suena más a un plan que ya tenías en la agenda. ¡Usá "will" para ser servicial!

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Identify the correct use of future for an immediate danger: "Careful! You _______ fall into that hole!"
questions.context: Una advertencia sobre un peligro inminente en una excursión.

options.feedback: "Will" would carry a distant prediction or an opinion, but here the danger is visible and about to happen.
For an immediate danger that the speaker can already see, English uses "be going to", so that completes the warning.
"Falling" on its own leaves the verb with no auxiliary, so the sentence is grammatically incomplete.
"Are falling" would mean the person is already in mid-air, not that it is about to happen.

questions.explanation:
Si ves que alguien está por pisar mal o tropezarse, la advertencia es con "going to". Es porque tenés la evidencia visual de que el accidente es casi inevitable. ¡Cuidado con los pozos!

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is wrong with this question? "When you will travel to Ushuaia?"
questions.context: Analizando errores en el uso de auxiliares para el futuro.

options.feedback: The -ing form is not needed here; the future "will" already carries the tense of the verb.

options.text: The word order is wrong; it should be 'When will you travel...?'.
options.feedback: In a question with "will" the auxiliary comes before the subject, so it must be "When will you travel...?"
"Will" can absolutely be used with "travel"; it is one of the most common future forms in English.
"Will" is already the future auxiliary, so it does not need the help of "do".

questions.explanation:
¡Ojo con las preguntas! No es como en castellano donde solo cambiás el tono. En inglés tenés que "saltar" el "will" adelante del sujeto: "When will you...?". Si no hacés ese cambio, la pregunta está mal armada.

questions.statement: Complete the complex sentence correctly: "As soon as I _______ (arrive) in Salta, I _______ (call) you."
questions.context: Un uso avanzado del futuro en cláusulas de tiempo (time clauses).

options.feedback: After a time connector such as "as soon as" or "when", the present simple is normally used, not "will".
With "as soon as", the time clause takes the present simple ("arrive") and the main clause takes "will" ("will call").
The rule works the other way round: it is the time clause that uses the present, not the main clause.

options.text: am arriving / am going to call
options.feedback: It could be understood, but the standard structure for this kind of time condition is present in the time clause and future in the main clause.

questions.explanation:
Esta es una regla difícil: cuando usás palabras como "when", "as soon as" o "until" para hablar del futuro, el verbo que viene inmediatamente después va en presente simple. Es "As soon as I arrive" (apenas llegue). La segunda parte de la frase sí lleva el "will". ¡Acordate de esto para sonar como un experto!
